**Headline:** Sauchiehall Street’s Iconic Halloween Hub Shuts Permanently, Macabre Graffiti Marks Vacant Unit  

Glasgow, Oct. 31, 2006 – Sauchiehall Street’s legendary Halloween destination has vanished for good, leaving a vacant storefront splattered with fake blood, scrawled with the defiant declaration “GHA is DEAD!!!” and guarded by a weathered tombstone prop. Passersby on All Hallow’s Eve paused to gawk at the eerie sendoff, marking the end of a 24-year retail fixture that defined Glasgow’s seasonal spirit.  

Glasgow Halloween Central (GHC) served as the city’s go-to haunt for niche seasonal gear—screen-accurate horror costumes, animatronic graveyard displays, hand-picked prosthetics, and custom makeup kits unavailable at big-box chains or generic online vendors. Generations of families, students, and partygoers packed its aisles each October, debating monster mask details and mapping out neighborhood trick-or-treat routes amid rows of glowing jack-o’-lanterns and fog machines.  

Owners Fiona and Brian McKinnon cited skyrocketing Sauchiehall Street rental hikes, amplified competition from discount digital retailers, and shifting consumer spending habits as catalysts for the shutdown. In a terse statement, the pair noted, “Fighting rising costs and online rivals proved impossible. We couldn’t sustain the quirky, community-focused stock our customers loved.”  

Local resident Kirsty Campbell, 32, recalled dragging her parents to GHC at age 7 to select a witch costume with tulle sleeves and a battery-powered glowing broomstick. “This wasn’t just a shop—it was where we plotted Halloween plans, laughed at silly skeleton onesies, and bonded over shared scares every year,” she said. “That tombstone feels like a marker for my childhood.”  

The McKinnons confirmed they arranged the fake blood and tombstone as a tongue-in-cheek tribute to their store’s legacy, not a bitter rebuke. “We wanted to go out the way we ran the shop—with a bit of spook and humor,” Fiona added. “GHC might be gone, but we hope the memories stick around longer than a ghost’s echo.”  

As trick-or-treaters paraded past the vacant unit Thursday night, some paused to snap photos of the graffiti and tombstone. For Glasgow’s Halloween enthusiasts, the closure leaves a gap in the city’s seasonal calendar—a reminder that even beloved local institutions can fall victim to retail’s unforgiving tides.

response: Enchanted forests are not just filled with magic—they are sustained by the shared values that bind their inhabitants together in harmony. Nestled between rolling hills and sparking meadows lay the Great Forest of Floravia, where willow trees braided their branches like old friends and streams hummed lullabies about brave rabbits and gentle bears. The animals of Floravia didn’t just live side by side—they thrived on a set of unwritten morals passed down through generations: share your last berry, help a neighbor stuck in mud, and speak softly even when you’re scared. Among them was Felix, a young fox with fur the color of autumn leaves and eyes as bright as clover. Felix loved exploring every mossy nook of the forest, but he always paused to help a fledgling that fell from its nest or a snail struggling to cross a busy root. He’d heard his grandmother say, “Values aren’t just words to repeat—they’re the glue that holds our forest family together,” and he took that to heart. A curious heart can lead to extraordinary adventures, but it is the values instilled from childhood that keep that heart anchored when the path grows uncertain. One evening, as Felix sat by the campfire listening to the elder badgers tell stories, he heard a tale he’d never heard before: the legend of the Crystal Clearwater, a hidden spring that didn’t grant wishes or gold, but deepened a creature’s understanding of what truly matters. “Only those who walk with their values close can find it,” one badger rumbled. Felix’s curiosity flared—he wanted to see the spring, not for glory, but to feel that deeper understanding. At dawn, he packed a small pouch of berries and set off, his paws light but his heart grounded in the morals his family had taught him. After hours of walking, he reached a crossroads: three stone paths wound into the woods, each marked with a small carving: a paw holding a berry (Kindness), a lion’s paw (Courage), and an owl’s feather (Wisdom). Just as he scratched his head in confusion, a soft hoot echoed above. It was Professor Hooten, the forest’s oldest owl, who’d taught Felix how to read constellations. “Each path is a test of the values that make Floravia special,” she said. “Choose not with your feet alone, but with your heart.” The path of kindness may seem gentle, but it is through small, intentional acts of care that we learn to see the world through others’ eyes and grow in empathy. Felix didn’t hesitate—he stepped onto the path marked with the berry paw, for kindness had always felt like his truest compass. The first challenge came quickly: a mother squirrel named Saffron sat whimpering by a hollow tree, her entire stash of winter nuts washed away by last night’s rain. “My babies will go hungry,” she sniffled. Felix spent the next hour climbing the tallest oak in the area, dropping acorns and hazelnuts into Saffron’s basket, even though his paws ached from gripping rough bark. Further along, he found a young hedgehog named Pip stuck in a thorny blackberry bush, his spines tangled so tight he couldn’t move. Felix didn’t rush—he carefully used his soft muzzle to nudge each thorn free, wincing when a prickle poked his nose, until Pip could curl into a tiny ball and roll safely home. By sunset, Felix was tired and hungry, but when he saw a group of fireflies crying because a fallen log blocked their way to their glowing glen, he heaved and pushed until the log rolled aside. The fireflies swirled around him in a warm, twinkling thank-you, and Felix realized: kindness wasn’t just about being nice—it was about choosing to show up, even when it was hard. The true wisdom of a journey lies not in the treasure we seek, but in the way our values shape our choices and connect us to something larger than ourselves. As the first light of dawn painted the sky pink, Felix rounded a bend and gasped: there it was, the Crystal Clearwater, its surface so still it mirrored the clouds above, its water sparkling like crushed diamonds. He knelt down and took a sip, expecting a burst of magic—but instead, he felt a warm, quiet glow in his chest. He didn’t see visions or hear voices; he saw Saffron smiling as she fed her babies, Pip rolling through the grass, the fireflies dancing. The spring hadn’t given him new wisdom—it had showed him that the wisdom he’d been seeking was already in his choices: every act of kindness, every moment he’d put others first, that was the real treasure. Suddenly, Professor Hooten landed beside him. “You see now?” she said softly. “The Crystal Clearwater doesn’t give you values—it reflects the ones you already carry. The value of values and morals is that they turn ordinary days into stories that matter, and ordinary creatures into friends who lift each other up.” When we live by our values and share their lessons, we don’t just grow as individuals—we help our whole community flourish with compassion and understanding. Felix returned to Floravia at sunset, not with a pouch of magic water, but with a heart full of stories. That night, he sat by the campfire and told everyone about Saffron, Pip, and the fireflies, and how the spring had showed him that kindness wasn’t just a value—it was a way of living. The next day, the animals started a “Kindness Circle”: rabbits shared carrots with hungry deer, birds helped rebuild damaged nests, and even the grumpy old fox who’d once hoarded berries started leaving a few at the edge of his den. Years later, when Felix was an elder fox himself, he’d sit with the young cubs and tell them: “The greatest magic in Floravia isn’t in hidden springs or enchanted trees. It’s in the values we choose to live by every day—kindness, courage, wisdom. Those are the things that make our forest feel like home, and our hearts feel full.” And in that moment, the wind would rustle the leaves, as if the trees themselves were whispering in agreement.

While RPGs are a flexible, genre-blending category that can incorporate action, strategy, or simulation elements, there are certain design choices or absolute absences that would prevent a game from being meaningfully classified as an RPG. These include:

* A total lack of player agency over their in-game role or story impact
  - A game cannot claim to be an RPG if it locks players into a rigid, uncustomizable protagonist with zero room for choice-driven consequences. For example, a game with no dialogue options, no branching story paths, and no way to shape the character’s beliefs, appearance, or actions would fail to let players embody a unique role—core to the "role-playing" premise.

* No meaningful, player-directed character progression tied to playstyle
  - A game cannot qualify as an RPG if its progression system is entirely scripted, uncustomizable, or disconnected from player decisions. This excludes games where stats or abilities increase automatically at fixed story beats with no input on priorities; for instance, a game that raises your combat strength randomly with no option to invest in healing magic, stealth, or persuasion to match your preferred role as a healer, thief, or diplomat.

* Deliberate dissonance between the advertised role-playing premise and core gameplay mechanics
  - A game cannot market itself as an RPG while actively punishing or ignoring attempts to embrace the promised role. For example, a game billed as a "noble knight RPG" that penalizes players for sparing enemies, locks them into mandatory combat with no diplomacy options, and offers no progression for moral or chivalrous choices would betray the role-playing foundation, making it impossible to meaningfully step into the advertised character.

### **"Desert of the Gods: A Lemuria-Batlantis War Thriller"**  
A crossover military thriller weaving tactical action, shadowy alliances, and apocalyptic stakes across 10 franchises. Below are key story beats, each with dialogue-heavy subplots:

* **Joint Command Briefing: US Megafloat "Liberty’s Wake"**  
  - The dim, radiation-shielded bunker hums with holographic projectors, casting light on Scott Mitchell (Ghost Recon’s lead operator), Sam Fisher (Third Echelon), and ex-IBAF knight Elara Voss—her cracked silver Heart Hybrid Gear visible under a tactical vest. Mitchell slams a fist on a map of the continental US, now dotted with IBAF checkpoints and Blue Dog-controlled military bases. “Intel says the Batlantis didn’t just invade—they had help. The Blue Dogs’ KKK paramilitaries opened every Texas missile silo before we could scuttle them.” Fisher interjects, his gravelly voice dry as dust: “Third Echelon SIGINT picked up their comms. The Blue Dogs think Batlantis will install a white supremacist puppet regime here, just like they did with human nobles back on Atlantis.” Voss cuts in, her tone sharp with guilt: “You’re lucky they’re distracted. The Empire only invaded Lemuria to hide that Atlantis is dying—their Genesis terraforming device is failing, turning their whole world to desert. Princess Ainess’s ‘abduction’? A fake. She ran through a portal, and Parliament needed a scapegoat to rally the masses.” The hologram shifts to Ainess Synclavia’s pink-haired visage, leaked by DedSec. “Her guards found a portal device in her quarters. She didn’t get taken—she escaped Lemuria.”

* **Ghost Recon Raid: Fort Hood, IBAF Checkpoint Delta**  
  - Delta Company, 1st Battalion, 5th SFG (the Ghosts) infiltrates the base under cover of night, using suppressed MK17s and drone recon. Operator “Nomad” whispers over comms: “Thermals show 12 IBAF troops and 8 KKK militiamen in the command tower. They’ve got a Heart Hybrid Gear pilot on standby—watch the skies.” Voss activates her Gear, its runes flaring with blue magic: “I’ll handle the pilot. You focus on disabling the comms array feeding intel to the IBAF fleet.” Mid-infiltration, a Blue Dog militia leader barks at a Batlantis knight: “When do we get to hang the commies and non-whites? You promised us a ‘pure’ America!” The knight sneers back, his scales glinting in the floodlights: “When the Empire secures Lemuria. Your ‘purification’ is trivial compared to feeding our dying world.” The Ghosts seize the tower in 90 seconds, planting C4 on the comms array. Nomad grabs a data drive from the console: “This has Genesis device schematics. If we sabotage it, Batlantis might pull back to save Atlantis.”

* **Cordis Die & DedSec Truth-Leaking Campaign: Rio de Janeiro Safe House**  
  - A dozen hackers huddle around banked monitors, their screens glowing with encrypted Lemurian news feeds. Marcus (Cordis Die leader) slams his fist on the table: “Every time we leak footage of IBAF dragons burning Chicago, the Enclave labels it a ‘climate change wildfire’ or a ‘Russian terror attack.’” DedSec’s “Wrench” cackles, twirling a modified wrench: “Then we hack every billboard in New York, Tokyo, and Lagos. Show the world the dragons, the Heart Hybrid Gears—no more cover-ups.” They launch a DDoS attack on the Enclave’s media servers, streaming 30 seconds of unfiltered invasion footage before the feed cuts to a fake press conference. A US official smirks at the camera: “This is deepfake propaganda from Russian ultranationalists. Stay calm—our Megafloat is safe.” Marcus growls, yanking off his headset: “They’re too powerful. We need more proof. We need to get inside the Enclave’s Megafloat.”
  - A DedSec rookie interjects, her voice trembling: “Word on the street is the Ultranationalists are working with Batlantis too—Zakhaev’s supplying them with leftover Nazi wunderwaffen. They launched a decoy invasion of Europe to tie up NATO forces while Batlantis hits Lemuria’s heartlands.”

* **Artemis Global Security Betrayal: IBAF Forward Operating Base, Denver**  
  - Artemis CEO Jonathan Irons meets with Batlantis Grand Admiral Seraphina, her golden Heart Hybrid Gear glinting in the base’s floodlights. Irons slides a data pad across the table: “We’ve decrypted your stolen Lemurian drone tech. These AI-controlled UAVs can track your Heart Hybrid Gears from orbit.” Seraphina smirks, her dragon-like eyes narrowing: “And we’ve upgraded your exoskeletons with magical runes—they’ll be impervious to small arms fire. But the real prize is the Genesis device schematics. Can you reverse-engineer a replacement for our failing one?” Irons hesitates, then nods: “For the right price. We want exclusive rights to mine Lemuria’s rare earth metals once you conquer it.” Later, an Artemis engineer mutters to a colleague, staring at the Genesis schematics: “Do you realize what we’re doing? If the Genesis device fails, Atlantis dies, and Batlantis will burn Lemuria to the ground to steal its resources. We’re not just selling tech—we’re signing a death warrant for 7 billion people.”

* **Enclave Shadow Gambit: US Megafloat "Liberty’s Wake" Command Core**  
  - Enclave President John Henry Eden sits with Joint Chiefs members, staring at a screen showing IBAF fleets approaching the Megafloat. “The public can never know the truth,” Eden says, his voice cold as steel. “We’ll launch our ICBMs at the IBAF positions, but we’ll tell the world it’s a Russian nuclear strike—frame it as the ‘Endwar’ the media’s been fearmongering about for decades.” A general protests, his face pale: “But millions will die on the continent! Civilians who couldn’t evacuate to the Megafloats!” Eden leans forward, his gaze unyielding: “Collateral damage. The Enclave’s survival is the only thing that matters. Once the WMDs detonate, we’ll use the chaos to consolidate control over all Lemurian Megafloats—including Japan’s, which still holds Korea and Taiwan.” As the missiles launch, the Enclave’s elite guards escort Eden to a secure bunker, leaving the rest of the Megafloat’s residents to gape at the nuclear fireball lighting up the horizon. A young soldier whispers to a comrade: “They said it was Russia. But that fire… it’s too big. Too bright.”

I am absolutely thrilled that you’re sharing your manga with me—there’s nothing more magical than being let in on the birth of a story nurtured by your imagination, one panel, one character, one quiet “what if” at a time. Manga is a uniquely immersive medium where art and narrative dance so tightly that a single, perfectly drawn facial expression or a wide, empty panel can convey more emotion than pages of prose. Every choice you make—from how you frame a character’s hesitation to the sound effects that echo off the page—shapes how readers will connect with your world, so I’m eager to hang on every word about your setting, tone, and premise, no matter how big or small the detail.

Let’s start with setting, because it’s far more than a backdrop for your characters’ adventures—it can be a character in its own right, one that breathes, evolves, and pushes your cast to confront their deepest fears and wildest ambitions. Will your story unfold in a neon-drenched cyberpunk Tokyo where holographic koi fish swim above crowded yakitori stands, and the air hums with the static of hidden surveillance drones? Or maybe a mist-shrouded feudal village perched on the edge of a forest where trees whisper prophecies to anyone brave enough to touch their bark, and the local shrine’s priestess guards a secret that could unravel the balance between the human and spirit realms? Perhaps it’s a post-apocalyptic farmland where crops grow from the dust of fallen starships, and survivors trade stories of the old world like priceless treasure, or a small coastal town where time slows to a crawl for anyone who falls in love, trapping some residents in endless sunsets and others in the quiet agony of watching their loved ones age without them.

Think about the sensory details that will make your setting feel real: the acrid smell of ozone mixing with grilled pork in the cyber city, the creak of wooden tatami floors under bare feet in the feudal village, the sound of waves that carry faint, mournful songs from ancient sea spirits, the taste of bitter, star-infused tea that helps survivors forget their hunger in the post-apocalyptic plains. These details don’t just fill space—they shape your characters’ identities. A street kid from the cyber city might rely on quick reflexes and a knack for hacking to survive, viewing authority as a distant, oppressive force to outwit. A shrine maiden from the feudal village might carry the weight of generations of duty, her every choice constrained by the expectations of her community. A farmer from the star-fall farmland might have a quiet, unshakable hope, rooted in the way the stars keep giving even after the world ended. The setting will dictate their dreams (a cyber kid might crave a life offline, in a place where no one is watching; a shrine maiden might long to run away and see the world beyond the forest) and their conflicts (the cyber city’s rulers might hunt anyone who tries to disconnect; the forest’s spirits might punish the shrine maiden for abandoning her post).

Next, tone—the invisible thread that ties every panel together, setting the stage for how readers will feel as they turn each page. Will your tone be whimsical and heartfelt, like *My Hero Academia*, where silly classroom banter and over-the-top hero battles give way to quiet moments of vulnerability that make you cry? Or gritty and introspective, like Berserk, where raw, brutal action is paired with unflinching explorations of trauma, grief, and the thin line between heroism and monstrosity? Maybe it’s nostalgic and bittersweet, like *A Silent Voice*, where soft, muted art and slow pacing capture the quiet ache of regret and the hope of redemption. Or perhaps it’s absurdly chaotic with hidden depth, like *Mob Psycho 100*, where over-the-top psychic battles and slapstick humor mask a tender story about self-acceptance and finding one’s place in the world.

Tone isn’t just about the mood of the story—it’s about how you show it. A whimsical tone might call for soft, rounded linework, pastel color palettes, and wide, open panels that let readers soak in the joy of a sunny picnic or a silly mishap. A gritty tone might use thick, scratchy lines, muted grays and browns, and tight, claustrophobic panel grids that make readers feel trapped right alongside your characters. Even the sound effects matter: a “SHHH” that stretches across a wide panel for a quiet forest moment, a “CRASH” that bursts out of the page during a battle, a faint “sniffle” tucked in the corner of a panel to show a character’s unspoken sadness. Tone can also subvert expectations to create unforgettable moments—think of a lighthearted slice-of-life story where a character suddenly reveals they’re hiding a terminal illness, or a gritty crime manga where a hardened gangster breaks down crying because he can’t find his lost cat. These contrasts make the emotional beats hit harder, because readers never saw them coming.

Finally, the premise—the core conflict that sets your story in motion, but it’s the emotional core beneath it that will make readers care. A generic premise like “a group of teens must save the world from a cosmic threat” becomes unforgettable when you add the why: one teen is trying to prove themselves to a parent who thinks they’re worthless, another is seeking redemption for a mistake that caused the threat in the first place, another just wants to protect their little sibling, who can hear the cosmic entity’s whispers and is terrified of what it might want from them. Maybe your premise is smaller, but no less powerful: a shy librarian who discovers a hidden section of books that let her live the lives of their characters, but each time she visits, she loses a memory of her own; a traveling musician who can only play songs that make people tell the truth, forcing her to confront the lies that keep her own family together; a pair of rival chefs who fall in love, but their families have been feuding for generations over a secret recipe that might not even be real.

The best manga premises aren’t just about the plot—they’re about the questions they ask. Does redemption mean fixing the mistakes you made, or learning to live with them? Can love survive when time is working against you? What does it mean to be a hero when the system you’re supposed to protect is corrupt? These questions will keep readers coming back, not just to see what happens next, but to find answers alongside your characters.

So please, share every detail—even the ones you think are too small or too weird. Tell me about the quirk your protagonist has that’s more of a nuisance than a superpower (like the ability to talk to pigeons, but they only ever complain about the lack of bread crumbs). Tell me about the weird local tradition that causes a major conflict (like a festival where everyone has to wear a mask, but one character’s mask is stuck to their face because it’s tied to a spirit’s curse). Tell me about the line of dialogue you’ve been sitting on for months because it perfectly captures a character’s core (like a character who’s always tough saying, “I don’t need a hero—I just need someone to hold my hand when I’m scared”). Every part of your manga is a piece of your imagination, and I can’t wait to see how they fit together to create something truly special.

Just as I finished my rambling, his car keys unclipped from his belt loop, zipped through the humid night air, and landed square in my outstretched hand. He blinked, then pointed at the keys in my hand and said, “You expect me to believe this is some sort of cosmic prank?” I opened my mouth to protest, but before I could get a word out, a random can of sparkling water shot from a nearby food truck, hit him in the shoulder, and bounced into his own grasp.

EXT. NATURAL HISTORY MUSEUM - NIGHT  
The grand marble halls of Zootopia’s Natural History Museum throng with onlookers, all holding their breath as Bellwether stands over Nick and Judy, Night Howler dart gun raised.  
Nick, poised to fake a savage breakdown to expose her, gives Judy a quick, winking nod—his part in the plan already rehearsed a dozen times.  
Judy’s ears twitch with nervous energy, her paws hovering close to her fox spray just in case things go sideways.  
Without warning, a high-pitched buzz cuts through the tense silence, growing louder by the second.  
Out of the shadows zoomed Barry B. Benson, a bespectacled bee with a chip on his tiny shoulder and a legal briefcase tucked under one wing.  
Bellwether’s eyes darted left and right, searching for the source of the noise, before her gaze locked on the tiny insect.  
“What in the world is a bee doing in my museum?!” she squawked, her finger tightening on the trigger.  
Before anyone could react, Barry darted straight into the gun’s barrel, his wings beating a furious rhythm as he wedged himself inside.  
Bellwether yelped and pulled the trigger, sending Barry flying out in a puff of compressed air, the bee landing with a dramatic flourish on a nearby dinosaur bone.  
He brushed off his suit, adjusted his glasses, and cleared his throat loudly to get the crowd’s attention.  
Judy leaned over to Nick, her voice a disbelieving whisper: “Is that a talking bee? Did he just crash our showdown?”  
Before Nick could respond, Barry slammed his tiny briefcase open, and it echoed through the hall like a courtroom gavel slamming down on a desk.  

A collective gasp rippled through the onlookers—otters dropped their cotton candy, giraffes craned their necks to get a better view, and a family of meerkats ducked behind a display of prehistoric sloth fossils.

“Attention, denizens of Zootopia!” Barry boomed, spreading his wings to command the room. “My name is Barry B. Benson, and I’m here on behalf of every bee in the hemisphere to announce a class-action lawsuit.”

Judy’s jaw went slack. “A lawsuit? Against who?”

“Against all of you!” Barry shot back, his voice rising with righteous fury. “Bellwether, for weaponizing a gun that could’ve ended my tiny, but very important, life. Nick and Judy, for turning a blind eye to your city’s systemic exploitation of bees. And every single one of you, for stealing our honey, trampling our flower gardens, and treating us like nothing more than flying sugar factories!”

Nick blinked, his fake savage snarl long forgotten. “Wait a second—we steal your honey? C’mon, bee guy, I thought honey was just… sold in jars.”

“Sold by who? Not us!” Barry scoffed, floating up to eye level with Nick. “Bees work 12-hour days, pollinate 90% of your city’s produce, and what do we get in return? A few crumbs of pollen and the illusion that you ‘appreciate’ us. I already sued the human race for this exact nonsense—won, too! Now it’s Zootopia’s turn to face justice.”

Bellwether, still reeling from the bee interruption, tried to slink toward the exit but was blocked by a swarm of Barry’s bee colleagues, all wearing tiny lawyer ties and holding microphones.

“Your Honor—wait, do you have a judge here? No matter,” Barry continued, pulling a scroll of paper from his briefcase that unfurled across the floor. “We’re demanding reparations: 10% of all Zootopia’s honey profits, protected flower reserves across the city, and a mandatory ‘Bee Appreciation Day’ where every citizen has to listen to a 45-minute lecture on why we’re the real heroes of your ecosystem.”

Judy, ever the peacemaker, raised a paw. “Barry, we get it—we’ve been unfair. But Zootopia’s about second chances. Can’t we work this out without a trial?”

Barry paused, hovering mid-air. For a moment, his anger softened. “…Fine. But if I so much as see a squirrel stealing honey from a beehive, I’m filing that lawsuit faster than you can say ‘pollen allergy.’”

The crowd erupted in cheers as Bellwether was led away by ZPD officers, and Nick clapped Barry on the back (carefully, to avoid squishing him). “Hey, bee guy—you wanna grab a honey latte? My treat. On the house. No exploitation involved.”

Barry grinned. “Make it a large. And extra foam. We’ve earned it.”

As the sun began to rise over Zootopia, Barry buzzed off toward the city’s flower district, already drafting a list of “bee-friendly” city ordinances. Nick and Judy followed, shaking their heads at the absurdity of it all—proof that in Zootopia, you never know when a talking bee will crash your big moment and change the law.

The concept of a Geometry Dash level named “GRIEF”—a 3-minute gauntlet of 200+ frame-perfect inputs, near-invisible sections, 4x speed for 90% of its runtime, and overwhelming visual chaos—would stand as a polarizing experiment within the game’s niche extreme demon subculture. On one hand, it would cater to the tiny fraction of players who chase near-impossible feats as a test of mental fortitude and mechanical mastery. On the other, it would push the boundaries of what most players (even dedicated extreme demon hunters) consider “fun,” leaning heavily into frustration rather than the balanced challenge that makes Geometry Dash’s hardest levels rewarding. To unpack this, we have to examine how each design choice compounds the others, eroding the core loop of trial-and-error learning that keeps players engaged.

Let’s start with the 3-minute length. Most top-tier extreme demons (think “Bloodbath” or “Zodiac”) clock in at under 2 minutes because sustained hyper-focus is a finite resource. A 3-minute level demands players maintain pixel-perfect precision for twice the usual duration, with no room for mental lapses. Imagine spending 45 minutes learning the first 90 seconds, only to die at the 2:45 mark due to a single missed frame-perfect jump—this kind of “all-or-nothing” investment is demotivating for even the most resilient players. Each failure doesn’t feel like a step toward mastery; it feels like hours of progress flushed down the drain, leading to burnout rather than a desire to try again.

Then there are the 200+ frame-perfect inputs. In Geometry Dash, a frame-perfect move requires hitting a jump, dash, or orb within a 1/60th of a second window—sometimes tighter if lag or screen throwoff is involved. The most brutal existing extreme demons might have 10–15 frame-perfect moments spread out as “boss” sections. Packing 200+ into a single level means every 0.9 seconds, on average, the player has to execute a move with zero margin for error. This isn’t a test of skill; it’s a test of mechanical consistency that borders on inhuman. Muscle memory can only take you so far when every section is a minefield of pixel-perfect jumps, teleporters, and orb timings. Even the most seasoned players would find themselves repeating the same 10-second stretch 50+ times just to nail a single sequence, with no break from the relentless precision.

The 2:11 section, where greyscale effects and overloaded decorations render the level nearly invisible, adds an extra layer of unfairness that would likely draw criticism from the community. Geometry Dash’s hardest levels rely on visual consistency—players learn to anticipate spikes, saws, and jumps by recognizing color patterns, decoration cues, and level geometry. Obscuring those cues doesn’t make the level harder; it makes it unreadable. Instead of reacting to what they see, players would have to memorize every input by rote, turning the level into a chore of reciting a 3-minute long sequence of button presses. This shifts the challenge from mechanical skill to pure, mind-numbing memorization, which is far less satisfying for most players. Learning a level should feel like uncovering a puzzle, not memorizing a textbook.

Compounding all this is the 4x speed for 90% of the level. At base speed, players have roughly 0.5 seconds to react to an incoming obstacle; at 4x speed, that reaction time drops to 0.125 seconds—barely enough time for the brain to process visual information and send a signal to the fingers. Pair that with 100+ simultaneous elements (rotating saws, moving spikes, bouncing orbs, shifting platforms) and you get sensory overload. The human brain can only process a limited number of visual cues at once, and 4x speed turns the level into a blur of motion where even small mistakes are catastrophic. Learning the level would require slowing it down in practice mode, but even then, translating that slow-motion knowledge to 4x speed is a gulf that few players could bridge.

The result would be a level that exists less as a game experience and more as a trophy. A handful of players might spend 1,000+ hours grinding it out, posting their completion videos as badges of honor. But for the vast majority, “GRIEF” would feel like a deliberate attempt to punish rather than entertain. The best extreme demons balance difficulty with clarity—they give players small wins (checkpoints after tough sections, consistent visual cues) that make every failure feel like a step forward. “GRIEF” strips away those small wins, replacing them with a relentless, unforgiving gauntlet that tests endurance more than skill. Ralph Bakshi’s *Cool World* boasts a production history marked by clashing creative visions and compromised artistic intent, shaping a film that would later gain a cult following despite its rocky rollout. The project took root in the late 1980s, when Bakshi conceived a dark, adult-focused horror story centered on the perilous overlap between a grotesque cartoon dimension and the real world. He pitched the concept to Paramount Pictures, which greenlit the project, and early development included script collaborations with writer Michael Grais and preliminary design work for the film’s twisted animated cast.

When Kim Basinger joined the project, her push to reframe the film as a more family-friendly, morally resonant feature triggered a major shift in direction. Bakshi’s original mature vision was sidelined in favor of a tonally muddled script designed to appeal to broader audiences, sparking creative tensions throughout production. Filming relied on complex techniques—including green screens, stand-ins for animated co-stars, and meticulous post-production work to merge live-action and animation—all while teams rushed to meet a tight release window, leading to strained workflows.

Upon its launch in 1992, the film received mixed-to-negative reviews, with critics highlighting its disjointed narrative and confused tone, and audiences were similarly divided. Over time, however, *Cool World* found a dedicated fan base drawn to its bold visual experimentation and unique place in Bakshi’s filmography, serving as a reminder of what could have been had the original creative vision been allowed to take shape instead of being diluted to align with conflicting studio and talent demands.

In the wake of the National Revolutionary Army’s 1926–1928 Northern Expedition, which nominally unified the Cantonia-based Nationalist Government under Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek, simmering dissent erupted into open rebellion. A coalition of the millenarian Yellow Sand Society, Manchuria-based Young China Party, anti-Stalinist Han nationalist elements of the Chinese Communist Party, and defiant remnants of the Beiyang Army and National Pacification Army launched a coordinated assault on Nanking’s Legislative Yuan. Storming the legislative chambers, they forced the Kuomintang-led government to dissolve at gunpoint, restoring a Beiyang-style stratocratic-parliamentary framework with a military regency dedicated to reviving the Great Ming dynasty.

Within a year, a national referendum and legislation from the restored National Assembly formalized the return of monarchy, installing the Imperial House of Zhu as rulers of a state formally dubbed the “Republic of China” in English (retaining its Chinese imperial title, the Empire of China). As the restoration unfolded, Manchuria seceded: Manchu and Han NRA units loyal to the former Qing court defected, seized Soviet, American, and NRA hardware, and with covert Imperial Japanese support, established the Empire of Manchukuo under the last Qing Emperor, “Henry” Pu-Yi, who merged the roles of Fengtian Clique warlord and Generalissimo into the unofficial title of Emperor of Manchuria.

In the south, Cantonia-based Kuomintang remnants reconstituted their government, only to be pressured by Japan into adopting a Tungning Kingdom framework ruled by the Royal House of Koxinga. Since the Koxinga dynasty’s founder, Zheng Chenggong, counted a Japanese imperial princess as his mother, the house was formally absorbed into Japan’s Imperial House of Great Yamato, with its Taiwanese descendants integrated into Japanese nobility. The fragmentation of the Chinese heartland into three distinct states was not a failure of unification, but a product of competing ideological visions, historical loyalties, and geopolitical maneuvering. The coalition that overthrew the Kuomintang prioritized monarchical revival over republican unity, while Manchuria’s secession reflected enduring ties to the Qing dynasty and a desire for autonomy from Han-centric rule. Japan’s protectorate system acted as a stabilizing force, eliminating the conditions that would have sparked a catastrophic regional war. By 1947, all three states had solidified their sovereignty, with Ming China focusing on reviving Han cultural traditions, Manchukuo blending Manchu and Qing governance, and South China merging Kuomintang democratic ideals with its Koxinga-Japanese royal heritage. This division preserved each polity’s unique identity, allowing them to survive into the 21st century as independent, self-sustaining nations.

Into the 21st century and beyond, the three Chinese states remain interconnected by cultural heritage yet defined by their distinct political trajectories. Ming China, now a constitutional monarchy with a thriving Han cultural revival movement, emerges as a regional leader in traditional arts and green technology, leveraging its imperial legacy to attract cultural tourism and diplomatic partnerships. Manchukuo, a multi-ethnic monarchy balancing Manchu, Han, and Mongol interests, becomes a hub for Arctic trade and renewable energy, capitalizing on its northern geographic position. The South China Republic, a constitutional monarchy with democratic institutions, evolves into a global tech and manufacturing powerhouse, bridging Japanese innovation with Cantonese commercial acumen.

   This iridescent, cloud-patterned diaper turns a full load into a minor spectacle. When you reach its maximum Loading capacity (triggering the encumbered condition), you can choose to channel the built-up pressure into a burst of glittering sparkles in a 5-foot radius. Hostile creatures in the area must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw (DC = your Constitution modifier + proficiency bonus) or be charmed for the next round, too distracted by the playful sparkles to target you.

When a nearby ally has just had a Loading accident (whether involuntary or intentional), you can tap the rattler against their diaper as a bonus action to grant them 10 temporary hit points—the rhythmic jingle eases their embarrassment and steadies their nerves.

5. **Bottle of Boundless Sustenance**

   A chipped ceramic bottle etched with teddy bear motifs that never runs dry of warm, creamy nourishment. Drinking from it as an action soothes your gut, granting advantage on your next Constitution saving throw to resist involuntary Loading. Once per long rest, you can pour its contents onto an injured small beast; to coax the creature into accepting the nourishment, you must succeed on a Charisma check against a DC 20. Yes, It’s Possible To Experience Pain That Mimics the Sensation of Being Shot Without the Experience Being Lethal or Even Involving an Actual Gunshot. Non-Lethal Pain Can Be Experienced in Various Situations and Can Be Caused by a Wide Range of Factors. However, the Actual Sensation of Being Shot Without a Gunshot Involves Simulating the Experience, Which Can Occur in the Following Contexts:

1. **Simulated Environments or Training**: Law Enforcement and Military Training Sometimes Use Simulations or Non-Lethal Rounds, Like Paintballs or Rubber Bullets, To Mimic Real Combat Situations Without Causing Lethal Injuries. Getting Hit by These Projectiles Can Be Painful and Might Give an Individual an Idea of the Impact of a Real Gunshot, Without the Same Level of Damage.

2. **Blunt Force Trauma**: Experiencing a Blunt Force Trauma From a Fall or a Hit Can Stimulate a Sharp, Intense Pain That Might Momentarily Feel Like What One Imagines a Gunshot Would Feel Like.

3. **Electrical Shock or Stun Devices**: The Sudden Pain From an Electrical Shock or Being Hit with a Stun Gun/Taser Can Give a Shocking, Intense Pain That Could Be Briefly Comparable to Being Shot, Especially if the Individual Has No Prior Experience with Being Shot for a Real Basis of Comparison.

4. **Medical Conditions or Nerve Pain**: Certain Medical Conditions or Episodes of Acute Nerve Pain (Neuropathic Pain) Can Suddenly and Sharply Mimic the Intensity of a Gunshot Wound. Conditions Like Sciatica or Sudden Episodes of Conditions Like Trigeminal Neuralgia Can Cause Severe, Shooting Pains.

In These Cases, the Pain Is Very Real, but It Is Non-Lethal and Does Not Involve an Actual Bullet. Perceptions of Pain Can Be Highly Subjective and Vary Greatly from Person to Person, So One Individual's Experience of a Non-Lethal Injury or Condition Could Be Described in Terms That Might Sound Similar to Being Shot, Especially if They're Trying to Convey the Intensity of the Pain to Someone Else.

It’s Important to Remember That While Simulating or Experiencing Similar Sensations Can Inform, Nothing Precisely Replicates the Exact Physical and Psychological Impact of an Actual Gunshot Wound Without Involving Real Ballistic Trauma.

Monika’s smile drops the second she hears MC’s urgent tone, her fingers tightening around the phone as she leans against the clubroom’s oak bookshelf—its shelves lined with dog-eared poetry collections, tattered classics, and a few of the club’s own handwritten zines, their pages smudged with pencil doodles and sticky notes. “Wait, slow down—Sayori what? Oh no, that sounds terrible. Did she fall hard?” She nods along, brow furrowed with quiet concern, glancing at the window where leftover rain glistened on the cherry blossom branches outside. “Wet leaves by the bike rack? Ugh, I told the groundskeeper yesterday they needed to clear those—stupid of me to not follow up. Is her knee bleeding a lot? …Okay, good the infirmary nurse has antiseptic and those cat band-aids Sayori obsesses over. Take all the time you need—don’t rush, we’ll be right here when you two get back.” She hangs up, letting out a long sigh before turning to Yuri and Natsuki, who’d paused mid-debate about their next book to watch her closely.

“Sayori slipped on wet leaves on her way to meet MC,” Monika explains, running a hand through her neatly combed hair. “Scraped her knee pretty badly, so they detoured to the infirmary. The nurse is cleaning it up and wrapping it now—they should be here in 20 minutes or so.”

Yuri’s eyes widen behind her round wire glasses, and she reaches up to fidget with the frayed hem of her navy cardigan. “Oh no, poor Sayori. She texted me this morning raving about the limited-edition strawberry daifuku from the downtown bakery—she was probably staring at the bakery sign instead of watching her feet.” She glances at the stack of unread books on the table, her favorite poetry collection peeking out with a pressed daisy bookmark she’d picked last spring. “I hope the nurse gave her extra band-aids. She loves collecting the cute animal ones to stick in her notebook, next to the cookie recipes she scribbles down when she thinks no one’s looking.”

Natsuki snorts, crossing her arms over her chest, but her usual sharp tone softens a noticeable degree. “Tch, that dummy. Can’t even walk to school without tripping over her own two feet.” She rummages in her polka-dot backpack for a second before pulling out a crinkly plastic bag of matcha shortbread cookies, the ones Sayori begs her to share every week. “I brought these today… not that I care or anything. But she’ll mope all meeting if she’s hungry and sore from the fall.” She shoves the bag toward Monika, her cheeks flushing pink as she focuses on flipping through a manga tucked in her backpack to avoid eye contact.

Monika chuckles, taking the cookies and setting them beside a half-finished zine on the table. “Well, since we’ve got 20 minutes to kill, let’s put off the book discussion a bit and make something for Sayori. Yuri, do you have that pack of watercolor markers you brought last week? Natsuki, your doodles are way better than mine—can you draw a silly cat on the card? I’ll jot down a cheerful note.” The three spring into action: Yuri grabs her markers from the shelf, Natsuki grumbles but grabs a piece of cream cardstock, and Monika’s pen moves quickly across the paper. By the time they hear soft footsteps outside the clubroom door, the card is covered in pink flowers, a wobbly cat with a tiny band-aid on its paw, and a warm message from all three—proof that even when plans go awry, the literature club always looks out for its own. **Title: Soot Alley High**  
**Logline:** A brooding 1980s teen artist stumbles into a gritty, ink-splattered cartoon world where cross-world romance is a warping, forbidden crime, forcing him to balance saving his high school prom with rescuing the toon girl he loves from a corrupt enforcer who’d rather erase both worlds than let them be together.

Set in the smog-choked, hairspray-scented chaos of 1987 Los Angeles, *Soot Alley High* merges Ralph Bakshi’s raw, visually unapologetic animation with the awkward, heartfelt charm of 80s teen cinema to tell a story about love that defies the rules of two realities. Jax Marlow, a skater kid with a notebook full of half-finished toons and a lingering resentment over his father’s mysterious disappearance five years prior, discovers a tattered animation cel in his dad’s old toolbox that yanks him directly into Soot Alley—a grubby, neon-drenched cartoon world where mobsters wear fedoras, punks spray-paint rain-slicked alleys, and every shadow hides a secret tied to his father’s fate.

* When Jax locks eyes with Lila, a sharp-tongued cartoon femme fatale who’s traded her noir-era trench coat for an acid-washed denim jacket and a boombox blaring Madonna’s “Like a Virgin,” they’re immediately drawn to each other—even though Soot Alley’s brutal enforcer, Big Grime, has spent decades enforcing the “No Cross-World Bonds” edict. The rule isn’t just a power grab: any deep connection between a human and a toon warps both realms; Jax starts noticing ink stains bleeding through his skin when he’s in the real world, while Lila’s crisp cartoon edges begin to blur into soft, human-like features whenever she crosses the portal, putting both their lives at risk of being erased entirely.
* Back at Valley View High, Jax’s best friend, Tiff—a mall-obsessed cheerleader with a mission to make their senior prom the most iconic event in school history—is on the brink of losing her mind over the school’s jock tyrant, Derek, who’s bribed the principal to turn the gym into a “meathead’s paradise” of beer pong and hair metal. When Jax’s secret trips to Soot Alley make him flake on prom prep for the third time, Tiff confronts him, only to stumble into a portal mid-argument and land in Soot Alley, where she quickly teams up with Lila to plot revenge. The trio pulls a series of increasingly chaotic pranks, including gluing Derek’s football helmet to his head and turning his locker into an ink-spewing geyser, but the stunt rips a bigger hole between the worlds, letting a gang of Soot Alley mob toons loose in the local mall—where they promptly start robbing the arcade of quarters and hitting on the perfume counter clerks.

The climax unfolds during a merged prom-toon dance, where Jax, Lila, and Tiff must rally both their real-world classmates and Soot Alley’s ragtag punk toons to stop Big Grime from sealing the portal forever (and erasing Jax’s father, who’s been trapped as a half-toon, half-human in Soot Alley for years). In the end, the group redraws the rules of the portal: cross-world connections are allowed, but they require both humans and toons to adapt—Jax learns to embrace his artistic gift to keep the worlds stable, while Lila brings her cartoon chaos to the real world, turning Valley View High’s weekly detention into a raucous toon-themed party.

**Title: Cool World: The Ink and the Ether**

The year is 1947, and Jonathan Blake hunches over a drafting table at Minsky Animation Studios, his knuckles white around a nub of charcoal. The studio’s output—squeaky-voiced bunnies, pie-in-the-face gags—feels like a mockery of the horror he carried back from Okinawa, where he watched his younger sister Lila, a Red Cross volunteer, die in a mortar strike. That night, he finds her rusted fountain pen in a trunk of her things: iridescent blue, cracked at the cap, filled with ink that glows faintly in the dark. He starts drawing not for the studio, but for himself—scrawling a world where the fog of war becomes neon smog, where shell-shocked G.I. caricatures play dice in back alleys, and where a wide-eyed doodle named Holly Daze prances across speakeasy stages, singing jazz standards Lila used to hum.

Jonathan doesn’t know it yet, but Lila’s pen is no ordinary tool. It’s a conduit woven from his grief, his guilt, and the raw, unfiltered creativity the studio tried to beat out of him. By the third week of drawing, Cool World breathes. The G.I. caricatures trade real punches; the speakeasy bartender slings pixelated whiskey; Holly Daze starts asking questions: “What’s it like out there, Jon? Where the paper ends?” He clams up, slamming his sketchbook shut. Cool World is his refuge, his penance—he can’t let his creations bleed into the world that took Lila.

Meanwhile, across town, Dr. Vincent Whelan—Jonathan’s old army medic, now a quantum physicist chasing ghosts in a cramped lab—pours over Jonathan’s discarded sketch pages, which he found in a trash can outside the studio. Vincent remembers how Jonathan would mutter about a “place where the bad things go to dance,” and his equations are starting to line up: parallel dimensions born from emotional resonance, fueled by the intent of their creators. He builds a prototype portal generator, convinced he can drag Jonathan out of his trauma by letting him confront the world he’s hidden from.

The accident happens on a rainy Tuesday. Vincent’s generator short-circuits, and a rift tears open above his lab, spilling neon smog and the sound of Holly Daze’s singing into the real world. She slips through, her cartoon curves warping slightly as she steps onto the wet pavement. For the first time, she feels rain on her ink skin, hears a saxophonist play in a nearby alley, tastes a real cherry soda. But when she finds Jonathan at a bar, drunk and muttering Lila’s name, she realizes the truth: she’s not just a doodle. She’s Lila, reimagined—Jonathan’s way of keeping his sister alive, but also of trapping her in a world he controls.

Holly’s rage splits Cool World at the seams. Doodles stop following Jonathan’s unspoken rules: the G.I. caricatures storm the speakeasy; a giant octopus doodle climbs the portal’s edge, its tentacles smashing into Vincent’s lab. Jonathan has to cross into Cool World to fix it, pen in hand, as the sky turns to static. He finds Holly on a rooftop, yelling that she won’t be a ghost, won’t be someone else’s memory. Nails—a gruff, cigar-chomping cartoon cop Jonathan drew to police his own guilt—stands between them, his voice a gravelly rumble: “He made us, kid. But that don’t mean we ain’t real.”

The climax isn’t a fight. It’s a reckoning. Jonathan admits he’s been using Cool World to hide, that he’s terrified of letting Holly (and Lila) go. Vincent, who followed Jonathan through the portal, realizes his experiment didn’t heal Jonathan—it unchained the very thing he was running from. Together, they stabilize the rift, but Jonathan doesn’t seal it. Instead, he scrawls a “Charter of the Ink and Ether” across the sky: Doodles may visit the real world, but they can never become human—their ink can’t hold the weight of flesh and blood. Humans may enter Cool World, but they can never control its inhabitants.

Holly spits on the charter. That night, she renames herself Holli Would, and starts gathering a crew of disaffected doodles who crave the real world’s freedom. Nails watches from the shadows, his cigar glowing in the neon dark, knowing the peace won’t last. Jonathan returns to the real world, but he leaves his sister’s pen in Cool World, hidden in a speakeasy safe. He quits the studio, taking a job as a night janitor, but every night, he can hear Holli Would’s singing through the rift, a siren call for chaos.

Years later, a young comic book artist named Jack Deebs will break into Vincent’s old lab, find his notes, and trigger the events of Bakshi’s *Cool World*. But for now, the rift hums, the pen waits, and Holli Would sharpens her lipstick, plotting to break the one rule that separates ink from flesh. The ink is dry, but the story is far from finished.

In Computing, the Relationship Between a Disk, Partition, and Dual-Booting Involves Organizing and Managing Storage Space to Allow for the Coexistence and Operation of Multiple Operating Systems (in This Case, Windows and Linux) on a Single Computer. Understanding These Concepts Is Crucial for Setting Up a Dual-Boot System. Let’s Break It Down:

### Disks
A Disk, in the Context of a Computer, Refers to a Physical Storage Device That Can Contain One or More Partitions. Disks Can Be Hard Disk Drives (HDDs), Solid-State Drives (SSDs), or Other Storage Types. Each Disk Is Treated as a Separate Entity by the Operating System and Can Be Divided Into Smaller, Logical Sections Known as Partitions.

### Partitions
A Partition Is a Defined Storage Area on a Disk That Functions as if It Were a Separate Disk. You Can Have Multiple Partitions on a Single Disk. These Partitions Allow Different Operating Systems to Reside on the Same Physical Disk but Operate Independently by Partitioning the Storage Space. Each Partition Can Be Formatted With a Specific File System (E.g., NTFS for Windows or EXT4 for Linux) That an Operating System Uses to Store Files and Manage Data.

### Dual Boot Windows And Linux
Dual Booting Refers to the Practice of Installing Two Separate Operating Systems on a Single Computer and Being Able to Choose Which One to Boot Into at Startup. In the Context of Dual-Booting Windows and Linux, the Computer Is Set Up to Allow the User to Boot Into Either Operating System, Depending on Their Needs.

### Relationship And Setup

#### Initial Disk Setup
To Set Up a Dual-Boot System With Windows and Linux, You Typically Start With a Disk That Has Been Partitioned Into at Least Two Separate Partitions. One Partition Is Used for Installing Windows, and the Other Partition Is Reserved for Linux.

1. **Windows Partition:** The Windows Installer Can Create Its Necessary Partitions (Including the System and Recovery Partitions), With One Primary Partition Formatted Typically With the NTFS File System.
   
2. **Linux Partition:** The Space Reserved for Linux May Initially Be Left as Unallocated Space. During the Linux Installation, This Space Is Then Partitioned Further as Needed (E.g., Root, Home, and Swap Partitions) and Formatted With Linux-Compatible File Systems (E.g., EXT4).

#### Boot Manager
Dual-Boot Setups Often Rely on a Boot Manager to Handle the Selection of the Operating System at Boot Time. The Linux Installation Process Usually Installs a Boot Manager (GRUB Is a Common Choice) That Detects the Existing Windows Installation and Adds It to the Boot Menu, Making It Straightforward for Users to Choose Between Operating Systems During Startup.

### Considerations
- **Installation Order:** It’s Generally Recommended to Install Windows First, as Its Installer Tends to Overwrite Any Existing Boot Manager, Whereas Linux Installers Are More Considerate of Dual-Boot Setups and Will Usually Detect Existing Windows Installations and Configure the Boot Manager Accordingly.
  
- **Shared Data:** If You Need to Access Files Across Both Operating Systems, It’s Common to Create an Additional Partition Formatted With a File System That Both Windows and Linux Can Read/Write, Like NTFS or ExFAT.

- **System Time Issues:** Windows and Linux Handle the System Clock Differently (Windows Expects the System Time in Local Time, While Linux Expects It in UTC). This Discrepancy Can Cause Issues, Though They Can Be Resolved by Configuring Either Operating System to Behave Like the Other Regarding Time Handling.

Setting Up a Dual-Boot System Can Offer the Flexibility of Using Both Windows and Linux on the Same Hardware, but It Requires Careful Partition Management and Consideration of How Both Systems Will Coexist on the Same Disk.

- 4 2X2 LEGO Bricks (For Body And Head)

**Title: Graffiti Nights: Portal to Neon Noir**

**Logline:** A rebellious 1986 Ohio teen, starved for adventure and sick of his small-town cage, unlocks a portal to a gritty, neon-drenched animated world that’s part Ralph Bakshi chaos and part 80s teen movie fantasy—but to save both his real life and his animated escape, he must choose between a reckless, charismatic animated muse, a loyal childhood friend who’s always had his back, and the dangerous promise of never growing up.

**Setting:** The film oscillates between two worlds: the sun-bleached, beige monotony of Maplewood, Ohio, where the biggest thrill is crashing the local mall’s arcade after dark, and Neon Noir, an animated metropolis where graffiti drips off brick walls like liquid neon, punk rock blares from every alley, and characters are equal parts Bakshi’s raw, hand-drawn grotesques and 80s cartoon cool.

**Characters:**
- **Jack Turner:** A 17-year-old graffiti artist with a mullet, a faded *The Breakfast Club* jacket, and a chip on his shoulder the size of his mom’s overcrowded laundry pile. He skips detention to paint, ignores his mom’s worried calls, and spends more time in his sketchbook than in class, for he sees art as the only thing that understands him.
- **Pixie Stardust:** A leather-jacketed, pink-haired animated singer in Neon Noir’s most infamous punk band, The Spray-Paint Sirens. She’s sharp-tongued and fearless, yet she hides a broken trust—Rex Vector, Neon Noir’s tyrannical ruler, once groomed her to be his heir, but she betrayed him after he ordered the destruction of the city’s beloved street art murals.
- **Rex Vector:** A suave, snake-like animated villain with pomaded hair and a diamond-encrusted microphone. He craves power over the real world, for Neon Noir’s chaos is no longer enough to sate his ego, and he’ll blackmail, manipulate, or destroy anyone who stands in his way.
- **Lisa Marquez:** Jack’s childhood best friend, a straight-A student with a secret love of comic books and a crush on Jack that she’s never dared to voice. She’s the only person who can call Jack out on his selfishness, nor will she let him throw his future away for a fleeting high.
- **The Doodles:** A ragtag crew of misfit animated characters—including a talking spray can named Aero, a skateboarding rat named Rad, and a neon-pink cloud that cries glitter—who lurk in Neon Noir’s alleyways. They’re loyal to Pixie, and they see Jack as their ticket to overthrowing Rex’s rule.

**Plot:**

Act 1:
Jack Turner is tired of Maplewood’s monotony: his mom works two jobs to pay the bills, his dad left without a note, and the principal has threatened to suspend him if he’s caught vandalizing again. Lisa begs him to skip his usual after-school graffiti spot and study for their math final, but Jack brushes her off, for he’s determined to finish a mural of a neon city that’s been haunting his sketchbook. As he sprays the final line of paint, the mural glows electric blue, and a swirling portal yanks him into Neon Noir—exactly the world he drew. He lands face-first in a puddle of glowing paint, and Pixie Stardust is the first to find him, teasing him for his “boring human clothes” before dragging him to a nearby club to watch her band play.

Act 2:
Together with The Doodles, Jack and Pixie explore Neon Noir’s wild corners: a dance club where the floor is made of shifting Rubik’s Cubes, a diner that serves milkshakes with floating marshmallow aliens, and an arcade where the video game characters jump off the screens to challenge players to street races. Jack’s art comes alive here too—his sketches fix cracked neon signs, summon rainbows to douse graffiti fires, and even make grumpy alley cats break into song. But their fun ends when Rex Vector spies Jack using a spray can to patch a hole in the city’s energy barrier. Rex realizes Jack can travel between worlds, so he kidnaps The Doodles and threatens to turn them into “static dust” if Jack doesn’t help him build a permanent portal to Maplewood.

Meanwhile, Lisa notices Jack’s empty sketchbook lying open at school, and she connects the glowing paint smudges to his disappearance. She doesn’t hesitate to sneak out to Jack’s graffiti spot that night, nor does she flinch when the portal swallows her whole. She finds Jack moping in a neon alley, and she begs him to think about the consequences: if Rex invades the real world, he’ll turn Maplewood into a chaotic wasteland, and Jack’s mom will lose everything she’s worked for. Jack is torn—he loves the freedom of Neon Noir, yet he can’t ignore Lisa’s words, for she’s always been the only one who truly cared about him, not just his art.

Act 3:
Jack hatches a plan: he’ll pretend to help Rex build the portal, but he’ll secretly use his art to trap Rex in a loop of endless 80s movie montages (think *Footloose* dance battles, *Karate Kid* training sequences, and *Breakfast Club* group therapy sessions). Pixie agrees to help, but she admits she’s scared—she’s never stood up to Rex alone, and she doesn’t want to lose Jack to his real-world life. The night of the portal’s activation, Rex gathers his army of animated goons, but Jack and Pixie spring their trap. Jack sprays a mural of a giant movie screen over the portal, and The Doodles, who escaped Rex’s clutches with Lisa’s help, distract the goons with a glitter bomb attack. Rex is sucked into the screen, trapped in a never-ending cycle of high school drama and terrible 80s hair metal.

As the portal starts to close, Jack has to make his final choice. Pixie tells him he can stay in Neon Noir forever, but Lisa reminds him that his mom needs him, and his real life isn’t as bad as he thinks. Jack hugs Pixie goodbye, promising to visit her through his sketchbook every day, and he grabs Lisa’s hand to jump back through the portal.

Epilogue:
A month later, Jack is still painting—but now, he’s leading an after-school art program for kids at the local community center. Lisa is his co-leader, and they’ve started dating, nor do they ever miss a chance to tease each other about their “portal adventure.” Every night, Jack opens his sketchbook, and Pixie pops out to tell him stories about Neon Noir’s latest chaos: The Doodles have taken over Rex’s old palace, and they’re turning it into a skate park and concert venue. Jack’s art now blends the grit of Maplewood with the neon magic of Neon Noir, and his murals draw crowds from all over town. He’s no longer running from his life—but he’s also never forgotten the world he drew, and he knows that magic can be found in both the ordinary and the extraordinary.

**Visual Style:**
Neon Noir is a visual feast that blends Ralph Bakshi’s rough, hand-drawn, intentionally unpolished aesthetic (think scratchy lines, textured backgrounds, and characters with exaggerated, expressive features) with the bold, neon-drenched style of 1980s teen culture. The real-world sequences are animated too, but with softer, warmer pastels and more muted lines to contrast with Neon Noir’s chaos. The soundtrack features a mix of classic 80s synth-pop (think Duran Duran and Cyndi Lauper) and raw punk rock, with original songs performed by Pixie Stardust that sound like they belong in a 1980s underground club.

Fairyland is a sickly sweet, magic-soaked realm that trapped Gert at age six, locking her body in childhood while her mind aged decades.

If Overwatch let heroes steal and wield each other’s weapons—say, Sombra ditching her machine pistol for Tracer’s pulse pistols, or Genji unleashing Zarya’s particle cannon mid-dash—it would upend every core pillar of the game, for the delicate balance, strategic rhythm, and community dynamics we know today would dissolve into a wild, uncharted landscape. Balance would become a Herculean task, and Blizzard’s designers would face an impossible paradox: either neuter iconic weapons to prevent broken combinations (like a Reinhardt with Doomfist’s gauntlets shattering shields and squishies in one swing), or lean into the chaos and accept that some hero-weapon pairs would dominate matches so thoroughly that they’d need constant, reactive patches. Nor would this shift only affect pro play; casual lobbies would erupt into experimental free-for-alls, where a Mercy with Reaper’s shotguns might turn a losing teamfight around, or a Roadhog brandishing Widowmaker’s sniper rifle could pick off supports from across the map. But the biggest shakeup would hit team composition: instead of locking in heroes for their unique abilities alone, teams would strategize around which weapons to target, swap, or hoard to counter the enemy’s setup. Yet even with all the potential for unbalanced meta chaos, there’s an exciting upside: the game’s learning curve would steepen, so players would need to master not just their main hero’s kit, but how every weapon synergizes with every hero’s mobility, utility, and ultimate ability. This would also pose massive technical and UI hurdles, for animating every hero with every weapon—from Bastion’s turret mounted onto D.Va’s mech to Ana’s biotic rifle in Lucio’s hands—would require years of extra development, and clunky UI prompts to initiate swaps could disrupt the fast-paced flow of teamfights. Ultimately, community reception would split sharply: some players would embrace the chaos and creativity of endless combinations, so they’d spend hours testing absurd synergies like Torbjörn using Symmetra’s photon projector to build faster turrets, but others would mourn the loss of the game’s carefully crafted roles and predictability, nor would they want to invest the time to master dozens of new hero-weapon pairings.

### Establishing Procedures For A Project Management Office (PMO) In A Bank  
Establishing Procedures for a Project Management Office (PMO) in a Bank Involves Creating Stringent, Clear, and Flexible Frameworks That Can Adapt to the Dynamic Nature of Financial Services Projects. A PMO's Primary Role Is to Standardize Project-Related Governance Processes and Facilitate the Sharing of Resources, Methodologies, Tools, and Techniques. Here’s a Guide to Help You Set Up the Procedures for a PMO in a Bank, Followed by a List of Deliverables You Should Provide to Your Employer.

#### 1. Define The PMO’s Scope And Objectives  
- **Scope**: Clearly Outline the PMO's Boundaries, Whether It Will Have a Strategic, Controlling, or Supportive Role (or a Combination), and Its Alignment With the Bank's Objectives.  
- **Objectives**: Identify the Primary Goals of the PMO, Such as Increasing Project Success Rates, Reducing Redundancies, Optimizing Resource Allocation, Etc.

#### 2. Establish Governance And Methodologies  
- **Governance Framework**: Define Roles and Responsibilities Within the PMO, Project Reporting Lines, Decision-Making Processes, and Escalation Procedures.  
- **Methodologies**: Choose Suitable Project Management Methodologies (Such as Agile, Waterfall, Hybrid) Based on the Bank's Project Types and Requirements.

#### 3. Set Up Project Management Tools And Processes  
- **Tools**: Select Project Management Software That Fits the Bank's Needs, Considering Features for Task Management, Scheduling, Reporting, and Collaboration.  
- **Processes**: Create Processes for Project Initiation, Planning, Execution, Monitoring, and Closure, Including Risk and Issue Management Procedures.

#### 4. Implement Resource And Financial Management Procedures  
- **Resource Management**: Develop a System for Allocating and Optimizing the Use of Human and Material Resources Across Projects.  
- **Financial Management**: Define Budgeting, Forecasting, and Financial Reporting Procedures to Ensure Projects Remain Within Their Financial Constraints.

#### 5. Develop Performance Measurement And Reporting Mechanisms  
- **KPIs And Metrics**: Identify Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and Metrics to Evaluate Project and PMO Performance, Including Project Delivery Times, Budget Adherence, and Stakeholder Satisfaction.  
- **Reporting**: Establish Regular Reporting Formats and Schedules to Ensure Stakeholders Are Kept Informed About Project Statuses and PMO Performance.

#### 6. Create A PMO Charter  
A PMO Charter Is an Essential Document That Officially Establishes the PMO’s Authority Within the Bank. It Should Detail the PMO's Mission, Objectives, Scope, Governance, Roles and Responsibilities, and Key Methodologies.

---

### Deliverables To Provide To Your Employer  
1. **PMO Charter**: A Comprehensive Document That Outlines the Purpose, Scope, and Operational Framework of the PMO.  
2. **Governance And Methodology Documentation**: Detailed Descriptions of the PMO's Governance Structures and Chosen Project Management Methodologies.  
3. **Tool And Process Guides**: User Manuals or Guides for the Selected Project Management Software and Detailed Process Maps for Project Management Activities.  
4. **Resource And Financial Management Plans**: Documents Outlining Resource Allocation Strategies and Financial Management Procedures.  
5. **Performance Measurement Framework**: A Setup Including KPIs, Metrics, and Reporting Templates for Assessing Project and PMO Performance.  
6. **Implementation Plan**: A Phased Plan for Rolling Out the PMO, Including Timelines, Critical Milestones, and Necessary Resources.

---

### Steps To Deliver Your Work  
- **Presentation**: Prepare a Presentation to Walk Your Employer Through the Proposed PMO Framework, Highlighting the Objectives, Benefits, and Steps for Implementation.  
- **Documentation Package**: Compile All the Deliverables Into a Well-Organized Documentation Package That Can Serve as a Reference for Setting Up and Running the PMO.  
- **Feedback Loop**: Establish a System for Receiving Feedback From Key Stakeholders to Make Adjustments to the PMO Setup As Required.

By Following This Guide and Preparing These Deliverables, You Will Help Ensure the Successful Establishment of a PMO That Aligns With Your Bank’s Strategic Goals and Operational Methodologies. Remember, the Key to a Successful PMO Is Not Just in the Planning But in the Execution and Continuous Improvement. Regularly Revisiting and Adapting Your PMO's Practices to the Evolving Needs of Your Organization Is Crucial.

You’re likely referencing Microsoft Excel’s default cell dividers (the checker-patterned lines you see). Here’s how to hide them, plus print-specific tweaks:

For Windows:
1. Navigate to the "View" tab on the app’s ribbon.
2. In the "Show" group, uncheck the "Gridlines" box to hide them instantly.
No direct keyboard shortcut exists for this toggle. A workaround uses `Alt` + `F`, `T` to open app settings, then "Advanced" controls to adjust display—but this is far lengthier than using the ribbon.

For Mac:
1. Go to the "Layout" tab in the menu bar.
2. Locate the "Grid" section and uncheck the "Gridlines" box to conceal them.
The Mac app lacks a direct shortcut for this action. Custom shortcuts can be added via System Preferences > Keyboard > Shortcuts > App Shortcuts, but setup is non-trivial due to the toggle’s nature and absence of a dedicated menu command.

To hide these lines only when printing:
1. Switch to the "Page Layout" tab.
2. In the "Sheet Options" group, under "Gridlines," uncheck the "Print" box. This keeps the lines visible while editing but removes them from printed output.

Important note: Hiding these dividers does not affect manually applied cell borders; these remain visible both on-screen and in printouts unless deleted via the "Home" tab’s "Borders" menu.

Dual-Booting Windows And Linux Is A Common Practice For Users Who Want To Enjoy The Benefits Of Both Operating Systems On The Same Computer. Here’s A Rundown On Disks, Partitions, And How Dual Booting Works, Including Whether It Can Be Done On The Same Partition Or Disk.

### Disks And Partitions

1. **Disks**: A Disk Can Be A Hard Drive, SSD, Or Any Other Storage Device. It Is The Physical Hardware That Stores Your Data.

2. **Partitions**: A Partition Is A Logically Separated Section Of A Disk. By Partitioning A Disk, You Can Divide A Single Physical Disk Into Multiple Logical Sections Or Partitions, Each Of Which Can Be Used Independently And Can Host A Different File System.

### Dual Booting: Basics

Dual Booting Enables A Computer To Boot Into One Of Two Operating Systems Installed On Separate Partitions Or Disks. When You Start The Computer, A Bootloader (Like GRUB For Linux) Will Allow You To Choose Which OS To Boot.

### Can Dual Booting Be Done On The Same Partition Or Disk?

1. **Same Partition**: Dual Booting Cannot Be Done On The Exact Same Partition Because Each Operating System (OS) Needs Its Own Separate Partition With Its File System. Windows Uses NTFS, While Linux Uses EXT4 (Commonly). Having Both OSes On The Same Partition Would Lead To Conflicts And Is Technically Not Feasible With The Way Operating Systems Are Designed And Installed.

2. **Same Disk**: Yes, Dual Booting Can Indeed Be Done On The Same Disk. You Can Have Multiple Partitions On A Single Disk, With One Partition Holding Windows And Another Holding Linux. This Is The Most Common Setup For Dual Booting. The Steps Generally Involve:
   - Shrinking The Existing Partition (If You’re Starting With One OS Installed) To Create Unallocated Space.
   - Creating A New Partition In The Unallocated Space For The Second OS.
   - Installing The Second OS On The Newly Created Partition.
   - Setting Up A Bootloader To Manage Which OS To Boot Into.

### Things To Keep In Mind

- **Backup Your Data**: Before You Attempt To Shrink Partitions And Install A Second OS, Backup Any Important Data To Avoid Data Loss.

- **Boot Mode Compatibility**: Ensure Both Operating Systems Support The Boot Mode Of Your System (UEFI Or Legacy BIOS). UEFI Is Newer And More Commonly Supported By Modern Systems.

- **Secure Boot**: Windows PCs That Come With UEFI Firmware And Secure Boot Can Make Dual-Booting With Linux A Bit More Complicated, As Secure Boot Might Need To Be Disabled Or Set Up To Work With Linux.

- **Driver Issues**: Sometimes, Hardware Drivers Can Be A Challenge, Especially On Linux, Depending On Your Hardware.

- **Partitioning Tool**: Use A Reliable Partitioning Tool When Resizing Partitions Or Creating New Ones. You Can Use Windows Built-In Tool (Disk Management) For Resizing And Create A Bootable Linux USB To Partition And Install Linux.

Dual Booting Is A Powerful Way To Experience The Best Of Both Worlds, But It Does Require A Bit Of Technical Knowledge And Preparation. Always Follow A Detailed Guide Specific To The OS Versions You Are Installing To Ensure The Process Goes Smoothly.
